summary:
Zonguldak is a province of Turkey and stands under the national framework set out below. No trans-specific statute, enforcement series, arrest pattern or incident record is documented for Zonguldak itself in the current source inventory. The absence of provincial reporting records an absence of documented divergence from national practice, not local safety: a visitor to Zonguldak is subject to the same national rules, the same document checks and the same policing patterns as elsewhere in Turkey.

At national level, a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years in prison, and would criminalise participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, carrying up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare, including surgery, from 18 to 25, conditioned on mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and patients up to three years, with pretrial detention possible. Human Rights Watch warns the package would force treatment underground and leave LGBT people in constant fear of arrest.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. As of the reporting date the package had not been enacted, but authorities have acted as though equivalent prohibitions were already operative, and street-level checks have been applied to trans people on that basis.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring review, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. Instructions framed around "the family" were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed for the first time in years, expression and artistic freedom were restricted, and events were cancelled or banned.

The same review records 6 right-to-life violations, including 3 hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected group. It records 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, and 313 liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the previous year's figure, comprising 299 detention decisions. Private-life violations rose from 16 to 67, including obstruction of trans people's hormone therapy, and 61 travel bans were recorded.

For a visitor, the practical exposure point is the identity-document interaction. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Police stop-and-check operations, documented in Istanbul in 2025, involved roughly 20 trans women held for background checks before release, with no fines issued but records taken. Every such interaction is an occasion on which a passport is compared against presentation, and a mismatch is an outing risk.

Custody conditions compound that risk. Turkey places trans prisoners according to registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison confirmed in parliamentary questions in December 2025. A transgender prisoner, Poyraz, was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025; rights groups demanded an independent investigation, reporting delayed medical attendance, prosecutors entering the prison two days later, and witness statements not taken. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer, no staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, binary administration, transfers that disrupt visits, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening in ways that reach records as well as treatment. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory recorded nationally has been consistently upward rather than episodic. Liberty violations roughly two and a half times the prior year, torture complaints rising from 51 to 89, and private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 all indicate a broadening enforcement and hostility pattern rather than isolated incidents, which means a visitor's experience cannot be inferred from a quiet spell.

The draft package and its enforcement sit alongside a rhetorical framework that Human Rights Watch identifies as the basis for legitimising stigma: protection of "the family" and "public morals". The formal closure of an LGBTI+ rights organisation in 2025 marks a change in the operating space for the domestic monitoring and support networks a visitor might otherwise rely on.

Turkey's trans-specific risks are comparable across provinces because the operative rules are national. The Istanbul data on street stops and Pride monitoring is the most detailed available, but the document-carrying requirement, registered-sex prison placement and the draft penal amendments apply in Zonguldak on identical terms.

Legal challenge routes exist but are unsettled. Legal experts cited in reporting on GBT checks argue they violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the Turkish Medical Association and fifteen LGBT groups opposed the draft package against regional-court precedent. Neither contestation has produced a suspension in practice.

The narrowing of transition care interacts with travel documentation. A visitor whose passport gender marker reflects a completed legal change still faces records systems that no longer permit an "other" designation, which raises the chance that any medical interaction or document comparison produces a discrepancy on file.
localsOnly:
Residents of Zonguldak live under the same national penal framework as visitors, but with continuous exposure rather than checkpoint-limited exposure: the 299 detention decisions recorded in 2025 and the 61 travel bans bear on residents' daily movement, employment and ability to leave the country.

Access to transition-related care is a resident-facing constraint. The Health Ministry regulation requiring e-reports and barring the "other" record option, alongside the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular adding "gender reassignment" as an official medical-board reason, channels trans patients into documented pathways and, if the draft package proceeds, would raise the age threshold to 25 behind a permanent-infertility mandate.

Residents convicted or detained face placement by registered sex in gendered facilities, with segregation and isolation as the governing practice rather than gender-matched housing. Trans prisoners are subject to arbitrary body and strip searches, restricted healthcare, transfers that break family visits and solidarity networks, and complaint processes recorded as ineffective.

Organising and public expression carry specific exposure. Events have been cancelled or banned under "Year of the Family" instructions to public institutions, an LGBTI+ rights organisation was closed in 2025, and artistic and expressive freedom was restricted, which affects residents' access to community gathering points as much as it affects public campaigning.

The record on hate violence is documented locally and pursued domestically. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation into the Sincan death, and opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised trans prison conditions in parliament on 12 December 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents a Zonguldak-specific arrest, incident, police practice, healthcare facility or local ordinance relating to trans people. Whether any provincial-level directive has been issued in Zonguldak following the "Year of the Family" instructions to public institutions is unresolved and not sourced here.

The 11th Judicial Package was reported as a leaked draft in October 2025 and, at that reporting date, had not been passed. Whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn is unresolved in this inventory; the penalties described are the draft's, not confirmed current law.

Figures for detentions, travel bans and violations in the Kaos GL 2025 review are national totals with no provincial breakdown available in this inventory, so the share attributable to Zonguldak cannot be stated.

Whether hospitals in Zonguldak hold a medical board able to issue gender-affirming care reports, and how the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation is applied by the provincial health directorate there, is not sourced.

The Human Rights Watch 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documents longstanding beatings, robbery and abuse of gay men and transgender people. It predates legal changes made after 2018 and is historical evidence of the regime's depth, not a statement of current law or current conditions in Zonguldak.
